content: Congenital herpes, also known as birth-acquired herpes, is a herpes virus infection that an infant acquires during the process of birth. Symptoms of Congenital Herpes: 1. Herpes may present as a localized skin infection. Small, fluid-filled blisters (vesicles) can appear, which eventually rupture, crust over, and heal, sometimes leaving mild scarring. 2. In some cases, the herpes infection can disseminate throughout the body, affecting multiple organ systems. This is referred to as disseminated herpes. 3. If the herpes virus infects the brain, it is termed herpes encephalitis. 4. Other organs, such as the liver, lungs, and kidneys, may also be involved. 5. Skin blisters may or may not be present in cases of disseminated herpes. 6. Newborns with herpes that has spread to the brain or other parts of the body are often critically ill. Symptoms in such cases may include: Easy bleeding Breathing difficulties Cyanosis (bluish discoloration of the skin) Nasal flaring Grunting Rapid breathing (tachypnea) Apneic episodes (short periods without breathing) Coma Neonatal jaundice Lethargy Hypothermia (low body temperature) Poor feeding Seizures Shock Skin lesions, including fluid-filled blisters Herpes acquired shortly after birth (postpartum) presents with symptoms similar to those of birth-acquired herpes. Intrauterine herpes, which occurs when the infection is transmitted during pregnancy, can lead to: Eye diseases, such as chorioretinitis (inflammation of the retina) Severe brain damage Skin lesions Causes of Congenital Herpes: 1. Newborns can acquire herpes virus infection through: Intrauterine transmission (very rare) Passage through the birth canal (the most common mode of transmission) Postpartum exposure, such as contact with someone who has active herpes mouth sores (e.g., through kissing) 2. If the mother has an active genital herpes infection during delivery, the risk of transmission to the baby is significantly higher. Some mothers may be unaware of internal herpes sores within the vagina. 3. Individuals who have had herpes infections in the past but were unaware of it may unknowingly transmit the virus to their baby. 4. Herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2, genital herpes) is the most common cause of neonatal herpes, but herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1, oral herpes) can also be transmitted. When to Seek Urgent Medical Care: If your baby exhibits any symptoms of birth-acquired herpes, including skin lesions alone, it is critical to have the baby evaluated by a healthcare provider immediately. Diagnosis: Tests used to diagnose birth-acquired herpes include: Direct fluorescent antibody (DFA) test for herpes (scraping from vesicles) Electroencephalogram (EEG) MRI of the head Spinal fluid culture Vesicle culture Additional tests may be performed if the baby is critically ill, such as: Blood gas analysis Coagulation studies (PT, PTT) Complete blood count (CBC) Electrolyte measurements Liver function tests Treatment Options: 1. Herpes virus infections in infants are typically treated with antiviral medications administered intravenously. Acyclovir is the most commonly used antiviral drug for this purpose, and treatment may need to continue for several weeks. 2. Supportive therapies are often required to manage complications of the infection, such as shock or seizures. 3. Critically ill infants are usually treated in an intensive care unit (ICU). Prognosis: 1. Infants with systemic herpes or herpes encephalitis often have poor outcomes, even with early antiviral treatment. 2. Infants with localized skin disease may experience recurrent vesicles after completing treatment. These recurrences can increase the risk of learning disabilities and may require further treatment. Possible Complications: Secondary bacterial or fungal infections of skin lesions Coma Death Developmental delays Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) and excessive bleeding Eye problems, such as chorioretinitis or keratitis Gastrointestinal issues, including diarrhea Hepatitis Jaundice Liver failure Lung problems, such as pneumonia or pneumonitis Neurological complications, including brain damage Respiratory distress Seizures Shock Skin lesions Prevention: 1. Women with a history of genital herpes should inform their healthcare provider. 2. Practicing safer sexual behaviors can help prevent the mother from acquiring genital herpes during pregnancy. Mothers who are not infected with herpes cannot transmit the virus to their baby during delivery. 3. Individuals with cold sores (herpes labialis) should avoid contact with newborns. Caregivers with active cold sores should wear surgical masks and practice strict hand hygiene before handling the infant to prevent transmission. 4. Mothers should consult their healthcare providers to discuss strategies for minimizing the risk of transmitting herpes to their baby.
